Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Her powerful voice resonates through the music hall, delivering an unlikely message of hope. All eight Liyana band members met at the King George VI school for disabled children in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe. The Afro-fusion melody comes from an unlikely source -- the small, wheelchair-ridden body of Prudence Mabhena, a woman from Zimbabwe who has overcome her physical disabilities and the hurdles of daily life in her home country. "Some people don't even get you and take you as a person," Mabhena said. "And with us singing right now, we're not giving up -- we're pushing up." Mabhena is the lead singer of Liyana, a group of eight musicians who are all physically disabled and from Zimbabwe. Their message of hope has been drowned out in their home country, which is suffering from an economic collapse, a cholera outbreak, and a political power struggle that has erupted into violence.  Watch the band performing » . Mabhena was born with arthrogryphosis, a muscle and joint disorder, and had to have parts of her arms and legs amputated as a result. She said her mother was told to kill her rather than have her face life as a physically disabled woman in Zimbabwe. Zimbabwe was once a center for disability rights after it gained independence in 1980, according to recent report on Public Radio International. It was one of the first countries to recognize the rights of the disabled, who are sometimes shunned by communities in rural Africa who fear they are touched by witchcraft. But the gains for the disabled in Zimbabwe have been erased by the country's current crisis, according to Dr. Raymond Lang of the London-based Cheshire Center for Conflict Recovery who spoke to PRI's Lonny Shavelson. Mabhena said the group is apprehensive about returning to Zimbabwe after its U.S. tour, which wrapped up this month. But none of the members of Liyana dwell on the despair. "'Never give up' -- it's one of our biggest and strongest mottos," said singer Tapiwa Nyenger, explaining one of the band's song titles. "We have the capability to go on stage and at the end of the day make people smile. It's a good feeling." All eight band members, who are between the ages of 17 and 23, met at the King George VI school for disabled children in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe. The band describes their music as a fusion between "myriad geographic, cultural, and musical genres including gospel, reggae, and traditional Zimbabwean Shona music." Liyana means "rain" -- a Shona term for good luck. "Music makes you think of something positive," Nyenger said. "For me, music is rehabilitation." Mabhena has said her voice is a gift from god. They had long dreamed of performing in the United States, and their multi-city tour included more than 20 performances in California and the New York metro area, including the New Jersey Performing Arts Center in Newark. "We have been received in an overwhelming, heart-filling way," Nyenger said. "Everywhere we go, every place we go, we [see] new things, we meet new people, we learn new stuff." The band's U.S. tour coincided with President Barack Obama's inauguration, which has also been a source of inspiration for a new song, "Obama." "When we heard Obama was going to be the American president, the first black American president, we were so excited," Mabhena said. "Through that joy that we had, there came a song." Liyana is also the subject of a new documentary, iTemba -- My Hope -- which is scheduled to be released worldwide later this year. The band's singers perform in seven languages -- Shona, Ndebele, English, Dutch, German, Hebrew, and Spanish -- allowing them to reach a wider audience. "We want to leave a message to everyone in the world that no matter what circumstance you are in, you can make it," singer Marvelous Meulo said.

All eight members of the band Liyana met at the King George VI School for Disabled Children in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe. The Afro-fusion melody comes from an unlikely source: the small, wheelchair-using body of Prudence Mabhena, a Zimbabwean woman who has overcome both physical disabilities and the challenges of daily life in her home country.

“Some people don’t even get you and take you as a person,” Mabhena said. “And with us singing right now, we’re not giving up — we’re pushing up.”

Mabhena is the lead singer of Liyana, a group of eight physically disabled musicians from Zimbabwe. Their message of hope has been drowned out in their home country, which is suffering from economic collapse, a cholera outbreak, and a political power struggle that has erupted into violence.

Watch the band performing »

Mabhena was born with arthrogryphosis, a muscle and joint disorder, and, as a result, had to have parts of her arms and legs amputated. She said her mother was told to kill her rather than have her face life as a physically disabled woman in Zimbabwe.

According to a recent report on Public Radio International, Zimbabwe was once a center for disability rights after gaining independence in 1980. It was one of the first countries to recognize the rights of people with disabilities, who are sometimes shunned by communities in rural Africa that fear they have been touched by witchcraft.

However, the gains made by people with disabilities in Zimbabwe have been erased by the country’s current crisis, according to Dr. Raymond Lang of the London-based Cheshire Center for Conflict Recovery, who spoke with PRI’s Lonny Shavelson.

Mabhena said the group is apprehensive about returning to Zimbabwe following its U.S. tour, which concluded this month. Nevertheless, none of Liyana’s members dwell on despair.

“‘Never give up’ — it’s one of our biggest and strongest mottos,” singer Tapiwa Nyenger said, explaining the title of one of the band’s songs. “We have the capability to go on stage and, at the end of the day, make people smile. It’s a good feeling.”

All eight band members, who range in age from 17 to 23, met at the King George VI School for Disabled Children in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe. The band describes its music as a fusion of “myriad geographic, cultural, and musical genres, including gospel, reggae, and traditional Zimbabwean Shona music.”

Liyana means “rain” — a Shona term for good luck.

“Music makes you think of something positive,” Nyenger said. “For me, music is rehabilitation.”

Mabhena has said that her voice is a gift from God.

The group had long dreamed of performing in the United States, and its multi-city tour included more than 20 performances in California and the New York metropolitan area, including an appearance at the New Jersey Performing Arts Center in Newark.

“We have been received in an overwhelming, heart-filling way,” Nyenger said. “Everywhere we go, every place we go, we [see] new things, we meet new people, we learn new stuff.”

The band’s U.S. tour coincided with President Barack Obama’s inauguration, which also inspired a new song, “Obama.”

“When we heard Obama was going to be the American president, the first Black American president, we were so excited,” Mabhena said. “Through that joy that we had, there came a song.”

Liyana is also the subject of a new documentary, *iTemba — My Hope*, which is scheduled for worldwide release later this year.

The band’s singers perform in seven languages — Shona, Ndebele, English, Dutch, German, Hebrew, and Spanish — enabling them to reach a broader audience.

“We want to leave a message to everyone in the world that, no matter what circumstance you are in, you can make it,” singer Marvelous Meulo said.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style human-interest news article about Liyana, an Afro-fusion band composed of eight young musicians with physical disabilities from Zimbabwe, focusing on lead singer Prudence Mabhena and the group’s message of hope.
counterfactuals.output:
# Zimbabwe’s Liyana turns hardship into a message of hope

**HARARE, Zimbabwe —** When Prudence Mabhena begins to sing, her voice rises with a force that seems to fill every corner of the room.

Mabhena is the lead singer of Liyana, an Afro-fusion band made up of eight young Zimbabwean musicians with physical disabilities. Together, they blend traditional African rhythms with contemporary sounds, using music to challenge assumptions about disability and to remind audiences that hardship does not have to silence hope.

For Mabhena, that message is deeply personal.

Born with arthrogryposis, a condition that limits movement in her limbs, she endured rejection and discrimination from an early age. In a society where disability can carry stigma — and where access to education, health care and employment remains limited — her path to the stage was far from assured.

Music became both a refuge and a way to be seen on her own terms.

At the King George VI School and Centre for Children with Physical Disabilities in Bulawayo, Mabhena found a community of young performers with similar experiences. Liyana grew from that environment, bringing together singers and instrumentalists who play marimbas, keyboards, drums and other instruments.

Onstage, the musicians are not defined by wheelchairs, crutches or physical limitations. They are defined by harmony, rhythm and the confidence with which they perform.

Their songs carry the energy of Zimbabwean musical traditions while drawing from pop, gospel and other influences. But beneath the bright percussion and layered vocals is a serious purpose: to confront prejudice and show what becomes possible when talent is given room to develop.

Mabhena’s story reached an international audience through the Oscar-winning documentary short **“Music by Prudence,”** which followed her journey and the band’s work. The film brought global attention to the challenges faced by people with disabilities in Zimbabwe, but it also emphasized resilience, friendship and creative ambition.

That distinction matters. Liyana’s musicians do not ask to be viewed only through the lens of struggle. Their performances are celebrations — of skill, identity and belonging.

For young people with disabilities, the band offers a powerful example. Its members have faced barriers that extend beyond the physical: inaccessible spaces, social exclusion and low expectations. By taking the stage, they push back against all three.

Mabhena stands at the center of that effort. Her voice can be tender one moment and commanding the next, carrying songs shaped by pain but not trapped by it. She has become a symbol of perseverance, yet her greatest impact may come from something simpler: being recognized as an artist.

Liyana’s message is not that adversity disappears. It is that dignity and possibility can survive alongside it.

Each performance turns that belief into sound. Eight musicians move through melody and rhythm together, transforming experiences of exclusion into a shared invitation: listen before judging, look beyond appearances and never underestimate where hope can lead.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a feature story on the disabled Zimbabwean band Liyana, covering how its members met, their U.S. tour, Zimbabwe’s political and economic crisis, and the documentary “iTemba — My Hope.”
counterfactuals.output:
# Liyana’s Long Road to Hope

In Bulawayo, Zimbabwe’s second-largest city, the musicians of Liyana learned early that making music was also an act of defiance.

The band’s members live with disabilities that, in Zimbabwe, often carry a heavy social stigma. Some use wheelchairs or crutches; others have conditions that affect their movement or growth. Yet onstage, those distinctions recede behind layered vocals, drums, keyboards and the driving rhythms of southern Africa.

Liyana emerged from the King George VI School and Centre for Children with Physical Disabilities in Bulawayo. Its future members met there as students, brought together by music classes and the school’s unusually strong performing-arts program. In a country where disabled children have often been hidden from public life or denied an education, the school offered both refuge and opportunity.

Among the group’s best-known performers was singer Prudence Mabhena, who was born with arthrogryposis, a condition that severely limited the use of her limbs. Abandoned by her mother and later neglected by relatives, she arrived at King George VI carrying experiences familiar to several of her bandmates: poverty, rejection and the assumption that disability made a full life impossible.

Music gave them a way to answer that assumption.

Liyana developed into a polished ensemble performing songs shaped by gospel, pop and traditional Zimbabwean sounds. The band’s name, associated with rain in the Ndebele language, suggested renewal in a country where hardship had become routine. Their performances were exuberant, but their very presence onstage made a larger argument—that disabled Zimbabweans should be seen not as objects of charity but as artists, workers and citizens.

## From Bulawayo to America

That argument traveled far beyond Zimbabwe when Liyana toured the United States.

For musicians accustomed to unreliable transport, inaccessible buildings and chronic shortages, the American journey was both exhilarating and disorienting. The band played for audiences who responded first to the music and then to the extraordinary circumstances behind it. School and community appearances turned the tour into more than a concert circuit: it became an exchange about disability, opportunity and the vast differences between life in the United States and life at home.

Accessibility was among the most striking contrasts. Ramps, elevators and adapted facilities that American audiences might barely notice represented a degree of independence largely unavailable in Zimbabwe. At the same time, the tour demanded stamina. Traveling with wheelchairs and other mobility needs is difficult even in countries with extensive disability protections.

The musicians also had to contend with a complicated public image. Their personal histories were compelling, but Liyana did not want sympathy to eclipse artistry. The band’s power came from the tension between those two ways of being seen: audiences could not ignore the obstacles its members had overcome, yet the performers insisted on being judged for what they created.

The tour brought international attention to the group and, especially, to Mabhena. Her life was later the focus of the Academy Award-winning short documentary *Music by Prudence*. But Liyana’s collective story was captured more fully in another film, *iTemba — My Hope*.

## A Country Coming Apart

The band’s rise coincided with one of the darkest periods in Zimbabwe’s modern history.

By the late 2000s, the country was in economic free fall. President Robert Mugabe, in power since independence in 1980, presided over an increasingly authoritarian system marked by political violence, repression and disputed elections. A chaotic land-redistribution program, shrinking agricultural production, corruption, sanctions and years of damaging economic policy contributed to a collapse that touched nearly every household.

Hyperinflation made the Zimbabwean dollar almost meaningless. Prices could change between morning and afternoon. Workers were paid in money that rapidly lost its purchasing power, while shops ran short of food, fuel and basic medicines. Electricity and water supplies became unreliable. Hospitals struggled to function.

The disputed 2008 presidential election deepened the crisis. Opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai won more votes than Mugabe in the first round but officially fell short of an outright majority. The period before the runoff was marked by intimidation, beatings and killings of opposition supporters. Tsvangirai withdrew, saying the violence made a credible election impossible, and Mugabe claimed victory. A power-sharing government was eventually formed, but only after months of uncertainty.

Then came a devastating cholera outbreak, fueled by failed sanitation systems and shortages of clean water.

For disabled Zimbabweans, every part of that emergency was magnified. Scarce medical care meant routine conditions could become dangerous. Broken roads and inaccessible public transportation restricted movement. Families struggling to find food were not always able—or willing—to support relatives who required additional care.

Liyana’s members therefore carried more than personal stories on their U.S. tour. They carried the reality of a country in collapse. While American audiences celebrated their talent, their families and schoolmates at home endured shortages, political fear and a public-health disaster.

## Hope Without Sentimentality

Directed by journalist and filmmaker Elinor Burkett, *iTemba — My Hope* follows Liyana through this intersection of disability, music and national crisis. “Ithemba” means “hope” in Ndebele, but the documentary’s hope is not soft or uncomplicated.

The film contrasts the excitement of the American tour with the band members’ lives in Zimbabwe. It presents performance as liberation, but it does not suggest that a successful concert can erase poverty, discrimination or political repression. The musicians return to a society where wheelchairs can be difficult to repair, buildings remain inaccessible and even basic necessities cannot be taken for granted.

That tension gives the documentary its force. Liyana’s members are inspiring, but the film resists reducing them to inspirational symbols. They are young artists with ambitions, rivalries, humor, frustration and sharply formed views about their country. Their disabilities shape their lives without fully defining them.

The documentary also turns the usual direction of scrutiny around. The musicians are not merely being observed by foreign audiences; they are observing America, comparing its abundance and accessibility with the conditions they know at home. Their reactions expose both the possibilities created by public investment and the injustice of treating such possibilities as luxuries.

## The Sound of Survival

Liyana’s story is ultimately about more than overcoming disability. It is about building community in a place where political and economic systems have failed many of the people who need them most.

The members found one another at King George VI because the school created space for disabled children to learn, perform and imagine adult lives. They reached American stages because teachers, organizers and supporters recognized that their music deserved a wider audience. And they became documentary subjects because their journey illuminated a Zimbabwe often described only through statistics about inflation, elections and disease.

Those statistics matter. But Liyana supplied the human soundtrack: young voices rising from Bulawayo while a nation staggered around them.

In *iTemba — My Hope*, hope is not presented as confidence that everything will improve. It is closer to persistence—the decision to rehearse when the electricity may fail, to travel when the world is inaccessible, and to perform before audiences inclined to see disability before talent.

For Liyana, hope was not an escape from Zimbabwe’s crisis. It was a way of insisting on a future inside it.

Through the support of educators, fellow musicians and her own determination, she developed her singing and emerged as the band’s leading performer.

Beyond her success on stage, Mabhena has become a symbol of inclusion and self-expression. # Against the odds, Zimbabwe’s Liyana is making music of hope

**BULAWAYO, Zimbabwe** — When the eight musicians of Liyana take the stage, they bring more than instruments and songs. They carry a message shaped by hardship, friendship and determination: Never give up.

The band was formed at King George VI School in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe, a school serving students with physical disabilities and visual impairments. For its members, music became both a means of self-expression and a way to challenge assumptions about what people with disabilities can achieve.

Blending Zimbabwean rhythms, powerful vocals and energetic performances, Liyana developed a sound rooted in the musicians’ lives and culture. Their songs speak of perseverance, dignity and hope — themes that resonate far beyond their school.

That message eventually carried the group across the Atlantic for a tour of the United States. Performing for audiences far from home, the musicians shared not only their talent but also their stories.

The journey was a remarkable milestone for young artists who had faced obstacles that could easily have silenced their ambitions. Instead, every performance became proof of what can happen when opportunity meets courage.

Liyana’s members do not ask audiences to ignore disability. They invite people to see the whole person: the artist, the student, the friend and the dreamer.

Their music also confronts stigma. In communities where disability can lead to exclusion or diminished expectations, Liyana offers a different narrative — one in which young people take control of the stage and define themselves through creativity rather than limitation.

The group’s success has inspired fellow students at King George VI School and listeners around the world. Its performances show that encouragement does not always come through speeches. Sometimes it arrives through a drumbeat, a melody or a voice rising above adversity.

For Liyana, touring the United States was more than a chance to perform abroad. It was an opportunity to build connections between cultures and remind audiences that resilience is a universal language.

The musicians’ path has not been easy, but that is precisely what gives their message its power. They know what it means to confront barriers — and to keep moving forward.

Through every song, Liyana delivers a simple refrain: Circumstances may shape a life, but they do not have to limit its possibilities.

And when the music begins, eight young musicians from Bulawayo show the world what refusing to give up sounds like.

counterfactuals.output:
## Liyana: music, disability and hope in Zimbabwe

Liyana is a musical ensemble formed by students and former students of the King George VI School and Centre for Children with Physical Disabilities in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe. Its members have included musicians with conditions such as arthrogryposis, osteogenesis imperfecta, muscular dystrophy and spina bifida, as well as performers who use wheelchairs or have limited use of their limbs. The group became internationally known through concerts, recordings and the Academy Award-winning documentary short *Music by Prudence*.

### The band’s name

**Liyana** means **“it is raining”** in isiNdebele. In Zimbabwe’s often dry climate, rain signifies blessing, renewal and the promise of life. The name therefore reflects the group’s aim: to bring hope and creative energy into circumstances often marked by hardship and exclusion.

### Members and outlook

The best-known member is singer and songwriter **Prudence Mabhena**, who was born with arthrogryposis, a condition that severely restricted the development and movement of her limbs. She experienced rejection and neglect as a child before attending King George VI School, where music gave her both a community and a public voice.

Mabhena has summarized her outlook with the statement:

> “Disability does not mean inability.”

She has also explained the personal importance of performance in simple terms:

> “I was born to sing.”

Those ideas represent the group as a whole. Liyana’s members do not deny the practical consequences of disability, but they resist being defined only by them. In interviews and performances, members have repeatedly expressed the view that music allows audiences to encounter them first as singers, composers and instrumentalists. A recurring sentiment among the musicians is:

> “We are disabled, but we are able.”

Liyana’s performances combine vocals with keyboards, guitars, percussion and Zimbabwean musical traditions. Adaptation is central to the group: instruments and playing techniques are adjusted to suit each musician’s range of movement.

### Multilingual performances

Liyana performs in several of Zimbabwe’s principal languages, especially:

- **isiNdebele**
- **Shona**
- **English**

The musicians may move between languages within a concert—and sometimes within a single song. This multilingual approach reflects Zimbabwe’s cultural diversity while also making the group’s message accessible to local and international audiences. Its repertoire combines gospel, Afro-pop, traditional Zimbabwean rhythms and songs addressing social or political themes.

### The Barack Obama song

One of Liyana’s best-known topical compositions is a song celebrating **Barack Obama’s election as the first African American president of the United States**. The musicians treated his 2008 victory not simply as an American political event but as a symbol of barriers being broken.

The song praises Obama as a figure of hope and change. For Liyana’s members, his rise carried a personal parallel: someone from a historically excluded group had reached a position many people once considered unattainable. The song therefore connects racial progress in the United States with the musicians’ own campaign against assumptions about disability. Its underlying message is that social prejudice need not determine what a person can become.

### Disability in Zimbabwe

Liyana’s story is inspiring, but it also draws attention to the severe problems faced by many disabled Zimbabweans.

#### Stigma and superstition

In some families and communities, disability is still interpreted as a curse, punishment, witchcraft or evidence of wrongdoing by a child’s parents. Disabled children may consequently be hidden from visitors, excluded from community life or abandoned. Prudence Mabhena’s early experiences—rejection by relatives and inadequate care—illustrate how dangerous such attitudes can become.

#### Limited access to education

Many mainstream schools lack ramps, accessible toilets, suitable transportation and teachers trained to support disabled pupils. Poverty makes attendance even more difficult because families may be unable to afford wheelchairs, medical treatment or transport. Specialized institutions such as King George VI provide crucial opportunities, but they cannot reach every child who needs support.

#### Health care and equipment

Zimbabwe’s economic difficulties have contributed to shortages of medicines, rehabilitation services, wheelchairs and assistive technology. Equipment is expensive to obtain and maintain, while specialist care is concentrated in urban areas. People in rural communities may have little or no access to physiotherapy or appropriate medical treatment.

#### Employment and economic exclusion

Disabled adults frequently encounter discrimination from employers, even when they have the necessary skills. Inaccessible buildings and transportation further restrict employment. As a result, disabled people are disproportionately vulnerable to poverty and dependence on relatives or charitable organizations.

#### Social invisibility and abuse

People with disabilities—particularly women and children—can be at greater risk of neglect, exploitation and sexual violence. They may also have less access to information about health, legal rights and personal safety. Because they are often excluded from public life, their experiences can remain unseen.

### Significance

Liyana is important not because its members have “overcome” disability in a simplistic sense, but because they have challenged the social conditions that turn physical impairment into exclusion. Their music presents disabled Zimbabweans as artists with humor, ambition, political opinions and cultural authority.

As Prudence Mabhena’s frequently repeated declaration puts it:

> “Disability does not mean inability.”

Through multilingual songs, international appearances and compositions such as the tribute to Barack Obama, Liyana transforms that statement from a slogan into a public demonstration of talent and belonging.
